name: Maipo Valley
shape: Chile Decreto 464, drawn from its comunas and provinces

climate: Summers are close to rainless. Vines draw on water stored in the soil, or on irrigation, but disease is rare.

keyfacts: It divides into three sub-regions: Alto Maipo, Central Maipo and Pacific Maipo.
Alto Maipo lies in the Andes foothills, where cold nights, hot days and poor, porous, rocky soil stress the vines and give bold, elegant Cabernet Sauvignon.
Central Maipo is the warmest and driest part, with rocky alluvial soils and drip irrigation, and Cabernet Sauvignon dominates alongside some Carmenère.
Pacific Maipo has coastal influence and alluvial soils, and is a popular place to experiment with white grapes, most notably Sauvignon Blanc.
Soils show high salinity from Maipo river irrigation and low potassium, and the valley sits directly across the Andes from Mendoza Province.

blurb.text: A subregion of the Central Valley, in the Metropolitana area, split into Alto, Central and Pacific Maipo. Cabernet Sauvignon covers 52 percent of its vines, well ahead of Merlot, Syrah, Carmenère, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay.
